title: How does gRPC load balancing work — why does a standard L4 (TCP) load balancer fail for gRPC (HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over ONE long-lived connection, so the LB sends all traffic to one backend) — and what are the fixes: an L7 (application-layer) load balancer that inspects HTTP/2 frames (Envoy, Istio, AWS ALB with gRPC support), or client-side load balancing where the client discovers backends (via DNS, service registry, or xDS) and distributes calls itself (`round_robin` / `pick_first` policies in the gRPC channel)?
shortTitle: How does gRPC load balancing work, why does an L4 load balancer fail, and what are the fixes?

s1_definition.profdef: gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which multiplexes many concurrent request streams over a single long-lived TCP connection. A layer-four load balancer balances at the TCP connection level, so once the one connection lands on a backend, every multiplexed request rides that same connection and only that one backend receives traffic, defeating load balancing. The fixes are either a layer-seven load balancer such as Envoy, Istio, or an AWS ALB with gRPC support that inspects individual HTTP/2 streams and distributes them, or client-side load balancing where the gRPC client discovers all backends through DNS, a service registry, or xDS and distributes calls itself using a policy such as `round_robin` or `pick_first`.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has one dedicated pneumatic tube between a branch and the processing center, and many request capsules travel through that single tube. A layer-four load balancer is like a clerk who only decides which processing center the tube connects to once, at setup, and then every capsule goes down that one tube to that one center, so the other centers sit idle. The layer-seven fix is a smarter clerk who opens each capsule as it arrives and routes that individual capsule to whichever center is least busy. The client-side fix is giving the branch the list of all centers so the branch itself alternates which center each capsule goes to.
s1_definition.oneliner: HTTP/2 multiplexing means one connection carries all requests, so an L4 LB pins them to one backend; fix it with an L7 LB that balances per stream or with client-side load balancing across discovered backends.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which multiplexes many concurrent request streams over a single long-lived TCP connection. A layer-four load balancer balances at the TCP connection level, so once the one connection lands on a backend, every multiplexed request rides that same connection and only that one backend receives traffic, defeating load balancing. The fixes are either a layer-seven load balancer such as Envoy, Istio, or an AWS ALB with gRPC support that inspects individual HTTP/2 streams and distributes them, or client-side load balancing where the gRPC client discovers all backends through DNS, a service registry, or xDS and distributes calls itself using a policy such as `round_robin` or `pick_first`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has one dedicated pneumatic tube between a branch and the processing center, and many request capsules travel through that single tube. A layer-four load balancer is like a clerk who only decides which processing center the tube connects to once, at setup, and then every capsule goes down that one tube to that one center, so the other centers sit idle. The layer-seven fix is a smarter clerk who opens each capsule as it arrives and routes that individual capsule to whichever center is least busy. The client-side fix is giving the branch the list of all centers so the branch itself alternates which center each capsule goes to.

**One line to remember:** HTTP/2 multiplexing means one connection carries all requests, so an L4 LB pins them to one backend; fix it with an L7 LB that balances per stream or with client-side load balancing across discovered backends.

sections.s2_technical:
The root cause is the mismatch between what a layer-four load balancer balances and how HTTP/2 works. A layer-four balancer makes its decision when a TCP connection is established and then forwards all bytes on that connection to the chosen backend. HTTP/1.1 opened a new connection per request or used a small pool, so a layer-four balancer spread load naturally. HTTP/2 deliberately uses one long-lived connection and multiplexes thousands of request streams over it, so the balancer picks a backend once and every request from that client goes to that single backend, leaving the rest idle. This is the classic gRPC load-balancing trap.

The first fix is a layer-seven load balancer that understands HTTP/2. Envoy, Istio, Linkerd, NGINX with HTTP/2, and AWS ALB with gRPC support terminate the HTTP/2 connection, see the individual request streams, and distribute each stream to a backend according to a policy. This gives true per-request balancing and a central place for retries, outlier detection, and observability, at the cost of an extra network hop and a proxy to operate.

The second fix is client-side load balancing, where the gRPC client itself knows about all the backends and spreads calls. The client uses a name resolver to discover backends, such as DNS that returns all pod IPs, a service registry like Consul or Eureka, or xDS which is the control-plane protocol Envoy and Istio use. Then it applies a load-balancing policy configured on the channel: `pick_first` tries endpoints in order and sticks to the first that works, while `round_robin` opens a subchannel to every backend and rotates requests across them. For example you configure `ManagedChannelBuilder.forTarget("dns:///account-service:9090").defaultLoadBalancingPolicy("round_robin")`, and in Kubernetes you use a headless service so DNS returns every pod IP rather than a single cluster IP. A senior nuance: round_robin needs the resolver to actually return multiple addresses, which is why a normal ClusterIP service fails and a headless service is required; you should also re-resolve periodically so new pods are picked up; and for large dynamic fleets, xDS-based balancing gives weighted and locality-aware routing that plain DNS cannot. In practice, service meshes combine both: a sidecar proxy does layer-seven balancing transparently so the application code stays simple.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs the account service as several pods behind a plain layer-four load balancer, and under load the team notices one pod is at 100 percent CPU while the others are idle. This is exactly the HTTP/2 single-connection trap — the layer-four balancer pinned every multiplexed request to one backend.

Problem 2 — The bank needs every account lookup to spread evenly across all pods and to pick up new pods automatically as they scale. This is exactly what client-side round-robin over a headless service, or an L7 proxy, solves — the client discovers all pods and rotates calls across them.

The demo shows a channel configured for client-side round-robin against a headless DNS target, a simple multi-instance account service to call, and logging that shows calls landing on different backends. Classes and steps: `account.proto`, `AccountServiceImpl` (reports its instance id), `GrpcServer` (one per port to simulate pods), and `BalancedClient` (round_robin channel).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Start THREE instances (simulating 3 pods) on different ports
java -cp target/classes com.bank.lb.GrpcServer 9091 &
java -cp target/classes com.bank.lb.GrpcServer 9092 &
java -cp target/classes com.bank.lb.GrpcServer 9093 &

# Client with round_robin spreads 6 calls across the 3 pods
java -cp target/classes com.bank.lb.BalancedClient

# In Kubernetes: a HEADLESS service is mandatory for round_robin
#   clusterIP: None  → DNS returns every pod IP (not one virtual IP)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: six balance lookups for Rajesh (SAV2001) against three account-service instances.

Step 1 — The client channel is built with target dns resolving three backends and the round_robin policy. The resolver returns all three addresses, so the channel opens a subchannel to each of pod-9091, pod-9092, and pod-9093.

Step 2 — The first call goes to pod-9091, which logs the lookup and returns the balance with served_by pod-9091. Had this been a layer-four balancer with one connection, every call would have been pinned to one pod instead.

Step 3 — The second call goes to pod-9092, the third to pod-9093, and the fourth wraps around to pod-9091 again, because round_robin rotates across the subchannels in order.

Step 4 — After six calls each pod has served exactly two, proving the load is spread evenly. In Kubernetes this only works because a headless service returns all pod IPs to DNS; a normal ClusterIP service would return one virtual IP and re-create the pinning problem.

```
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9091 balance=Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9092 balance=Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9093 balance=Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9091 balance=Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9092 balance=Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 15:35:02 [INFO] served_by=pod-9093 balance=Rs.1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  THE PROBLEM (L4 / TCP load balancer)
    Client ── ONE HTTP/2 connection ──► L4 LB ──► pod-9091  (100% CPU)
                                                  pod-9092  (idle)
                                                  pod-9093  (idle)
    multiplexed streams all ride the one connection → pinned to one backend

  THE FIX A (L7 proxy inspects HTTP/2 frames)
    Client ──► Envoy/Istio/ALB ──stream 1──► pod-9091
                              ──stream 2──► pod-9092
                              ──stream 3──► pod-9093   (per-request balancing)

  THE FIX B (client-side round_robin)
    resolver dns:/// → [9091, 9092, 9093]
    Client channel opens a subchannel to EACH backend
      call 1 → 9091 ; call 2 → 9092 ; call 3 → 9093 ; call 4 → 9091 ...
    (needs HEADLESS service so DNS returns all pod IPs)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — gRPC Channel LB Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: LB policy (round_robin / pick_first) on the channel  │
  │    WHY: swap balancing behavior without changing call code     │
  │ Name Resolver: dns / xds / registry → list of backends         │
  │    WHY: decouple "who are the backends" from "how to pick one" │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: resolver discovers; policy distributes — one job each       │
  │ O: new policy (weighted) = new strategy, no call-site changes  │
  │ D: client depends on channel abstraction, not on backend IPs   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Why L4 Fails / How Fixes Work (as prose) ──────────────────
  L4 fail     : balances at TCP; 1 HTTP/2 conn = all streams → 1 pod
  L7 fix      : terminates HTTP/2, balances each stream (Envoy/Istio/ALB)
  client-side : resolver returns all IPs; round_robin rotates subchannels
  pick_first  : stick to first working endpoint (no spread)
  K8s need    : headless Service (clusterIP None) so DNS returns all pods

  ── Call Chain (client-side round_robin) ──────────────────────
  1. channel.forTarget("dns:///...") + round_robin
  2.   → resolver returns [9091, 9092, 9093]
  3.   → open subchannel to each backend
  4.   → call N → subchannel[N mod 3] → even spread
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason gRPC load balancing is tricky is a mismatch between how a standard load balancer works and how HTTP/2 works. gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which deliberately uses one long-lived TCP connection and multiplexes thousands of request streams over it. A layer-four, or TCP, load balancer makes its routing decision once, when the connection is established, and then every byte on that connection goes to the chosen backend. So with gRPC, the balancer picks one backend and every multiplexed request from that client lands on that single backend, while the others sit idle. That is the classic trap, and it is exactly what I have seen in production when one pod is pegged at full CPU and the rest are quiet.

There are two fixes. The first is a layer-seven load balancer that understands HTTP/2, like Envoy, Istio, Linkerd, or an AWS ALB with gRPC support. It terminates the HTTP/2 connection, sees the individual request streams, and distributes each stream to a backend, which gives true per-request balancing plus a central place for retries and observability, at the cost of an extra hop and a proxy to run.

The second fix is client-side load balancing, where the gRPC client itself knows all the backends and spreads the calls. The client uses a name resolver to discover them, through DNS that returns all pod IPs, a service registry, or xDS, and then applies a policy on the channel. pick_first just sticks to the first working endpoint, but round_robin opens a subchannel to every backend and rotates requests across them. I configure the channel target as a dns address and set the default load-balancing policy to round_robin.

In my banking work at National Bank of India the account service ran as several pods, and we used client-side round-robin so every balance lookup spread evenly and new pods were picked up as they scaled. The single most important senior detail I always stress is that round_robin only works if the resolver actually returns multiple addresses, so in Kubernetes a normal ClusterIP service breaks it by returning one virtual IP and re-creating the pinning, and you must use a headless service so DNS returns every pod IP. In larger meshes we let a sidecar proxy do layer-seven balancing transparently so the application code stayed simple, and for big dynamic fleets xDS gives weighted and locality-aware routing that plain DNS cannot.
